title: Dial Lookup
statement: A combination dial lists distinct numbers that were sorted in increasing order and then rotated: some prefix was moved to the end, so [10, 20, 30, 40, 50] might be stored as [40, 50, 10, 20, 30]. The rotation may also be zero. Given dial and a target, return the index of target in dial, or -1 if it is absent. Aim for logarithmic time.
constraints: dial values are distinct and form a rotated increasing sequence

hints.content: A linear scan works, but the array is almost sorted.
Cut the array at any middle index: at least one of the two halves is sorted in the ordinary way.
You can tell which half is sorted by comparing the middle value with the value at the left end.
If the target lies within the sorted half's value range, search that half; otherwise search the other half.

Use inclusive bounds: when dial[lo] <= dial[mid], the left half [lo, mid] is sorted, so check dial[lo] <= target < dial[mid]. Otherwise the right half is sorted, so check dial[mid] < target <= dial[hi].

testCases.explanation: A single value that does not match.
The largest value sits at index 0.
The smallest value sits at the end.
Negative values on the wrapped side.
A value that falls between existing numbers is absent.

solutions.title: Linear scan
solutions.intuition: Look at every position until the target appears.
solutions.approach: Loop over indices and return the first index whose value equals target, or -1.
solutions.pseudocode:
for i in 0..n-1: if dial[i] == target: return i
return -1
commonMistakes: Returning the value instead of the index.
solutions.interviewExplanation: A scan is always correct but ignores the rotated-sorted structure that allows logarithmic search.

solutions.title: Binary search on the sorted half
solutions.intuition: Every split of a rotated sorted array has at least one ordinary sorted half, and a sorted half lets you decide in O(1) whether the target can be there.
solutions.approach: Keep lo and hi. Compute mid; return it if it matches. If dial[lo] <= dial[mid], the left half is sorted: move hi to mid - 1 when target is within [dial[lo], dial[mid]), otherwise move lo to mid + 1. Otherwise the right half is sorted: move lo to mid + 1 when target is within (dial[mid], dial[hi]], otherwise move hi to mid - 1.
solutions.pseudocode:
lo = 0; hi = n - 1
while lo <= hi: mid = (lo + hi) / 2; if dial[mid] == target: return mid
  if dial[lo] <= dial[mid]: if dial[lo] <= target < dial[mid]: hi = mid - 1 else lo = mid + 1
  else: if dial[mid] < target <= dial[hi]: lo = mid + 1 else hi = mid - 1
return -1
commonMistakes: Using dial[lo] < dial[mid] when lo == mid, which misclassifies a one-element left half.
Testing the target against the unsorted half's endpoints, which says nothing about where it lies.
solutions.interviewExplanation: I run binary search but first ask which half is normally sorted. Comparing dial[lo] with dial[mid] tells me. If the target falls within the sorted half's range I keep that half, otherwise the other, so each step discards half the array and the search is O(log n). The <= in dial[lo] <= dial[mid] matters when lo equals mid.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: lo=0, hi=4, mid=2 (10). dial[0]=40 > 10, so the right half [10,20,30] is sorted, and 20 is in (10, 30], so lo = 3.
